subject: scale the precision matrix in Generic0 for PC prior

messages.author: 80b903b54c9cf4bd
messages.subject: scale the precision matrix in Generic0 for PC prior
parts:
I'm trying to use inla.scale.model to scale a customized precision matrix, since the Generic0 does not provide the feature.

Suppose I have a precision matrix Q.s for spatial effect (ICAR model), which is rank S-1 (sum-to-zero constraint will be needed). Also, I have precision matrix  Q.t for (rw2) temporal effect, with is rank T-2. 

Then the interaction term can have a precision matrix
R =kronecker(Q.t,Q.s)
#rank deficiency for R
r.def =2*S+T-2
A1 = kronecker(matrix(1, 1,T),diag(S))
A2 = kronecker(diag(T), matrix(1, 1, S))
A.constr =rbind(A1, A2）
#formular for the interaction term
...~ ...+f(ID.area.year, model="generic0", Cmatrix=R, rankdef=r.def, constr=TRUE, hyper=list(prec=list(prior=<some prior>), extraconstr=list(A=A.constr, e=rep(0, S+T))))
So by constr=TRUE, the overall sum to zero constraint was added. The other constraints were added by extraconstr argument.

So how should I use those information to scale my matrix Rin generic0 model(I want to use PC prior)? Since there is no  constr=TRUE argument in inla.scale.model, I'm assuming I need to manually add the sum-to-zero constraint
n = dim(R)[1]
Anew = rbind(matrix(1, 1, n), A.constr)
> R.scaled = inla.scale.model(R, constr = list(A = Anew, e=rep(0, nrow(Anew))))
x[.,.] <- val : x being coerced from Tsparse* to CsparseMatrix
1. Is that the correct way doing the job? Should the constraints be the same as those used for modeling? Or should I just use one constraint?
inla.scale.model(R, constr = list(A = matrix(1, 1, n), e=0))

2. I noticed the rank of R.scaled is the same as R. Should I fit the scaled model using the same formular like
...~ ...+f(ID.area.year, model="generic0", Cmatrix=R.scaled, rankdef=r.def, constr=TRUE, hyper=list(prec=list(prior=<some prior>), extraconstr=list(A=A.constr, e=rep(0, S+T))))


Thanks,

Jiang

On Mon, 2017-12-18 at 13:41 -0800, Jiang Du wrote:
> I'm trying to use inla.scale.model to scale a customized precision
> matrix, since the Generic0 does not provide the feature.
>
> Suppose I have a precision matrix Q.s for spatial effect (ICAR
> model), which is rank S-1 (sum-to-zero constraint will be needed).
> Also, I have precision matrix Q.t for (rw2) temporal effect, with is
> rank T-2.
>
> Then the interaction term can have a precision matrix
> R =kronecker(Q.t,Q.s)
> #rank deficiency for R
> r.def =2*S+T-2
> A1 = kronecker(matrix(1, 1,T),diag(S))
> A2 = kronecker(diag(T), matrix(1, 1, S))
> A.constr =rbind(A1, A2）
> #formular for the interaction term
> ...~ ...+f(ID.area.year, model="generic0", Cmatrix=R, rankdef=r.def,
> constr=TRUE, hyper=list(prec=list(prior=<some prior>),
> extraconstr=list(A=A.constr, e=rep(0, S+T))))
> So by constr=TRUE, the overall sum to zero constraint was added. The
> other constraints were added by extraconstr argument.
>
> So how should I use those information to scale my matrix Rin generic0
> model(I want to use PC prior)?

To use 'inla.scale.model', you have to define the 'constr' argument,
which defines the null space. I think this is what you do in your code.
This approach will work for models of large/huge size, since we can
'correct' for the constraints.

There is also an easier approach, which works (only) for smaller
models, which is just computing the generalized inverse (an O(n^3)
operation which we normally try to avoid), and even more robust, if you
know the rank deficiency, like this

> Q = INLA:::inla.rw(10, order = 2)
> S = INLA:::inla.ginv(Q, rankdef = 2)
> exp(mean(log(diag(S))))
[1] 1.818652956

and then you can scale it with 's'

> s = exp(mean(log(diag(S))))
> Q = s * Q
> S = INLA:::inla.ginv(Q, rankdef = 2)
> exp(mean(log(diag(S))))
[1] 1
> 1. Is that the correct way doing the job?

Yes, you have to add all the constraints in 'constr' when calling
inla.scale.model

> Q = INLA:::inla.rw(10, order = 2)
> constr = list(A = rbind(rep(1,10), 1:10), e = c(0,0))
> QQ = inla.scale.model(Q, constr)
> QQ[1,1] / Q[1]
[1] 1.818650644

the 'same' scaling factor applied.

> 2. I noticed the rank of R.scaled is the same as R. Should I fit the
> scaled model using the same formular like
> ...~ ...+f(ID.area.year, model="generic0", Cmatrix=R.scaled, rankdef=

> r.def, constr=TRUE, hyper=list(prec=list(prior=<some
> prior>), extraconstr=list(A=A.constr, e=rep(0, S+T))))

you can if you like, but this depends on your model.
at least, give the 'rankdef' as there
is no way to know this without doing an expensive calculation.
if you want to lock-down the null-space, you have to
use the (extra)constr like this. you can also
set constr=F and add the sum-to-zero constr in 'extraconstr' (otherwise, it is added
internally)


Best
H



--

Thank you for the detailed reply. Calculating the generalized variance and then scale the precision matrix makes sense to me. Earlier I had an update but I'm not sure if you have received that. I will first copy my earlier update and then, may I ask how the two approaches different?

First part:

The generalized variance is not 1 after my calculation above using the constraints during same as formula. After reading the paper
An intuitive Bayesian spatial model for disease mapping that accounts for scaling
more carefully, I came up with the following code, this time, the generalized variance is around 1. However, I don't know if I'm doing correctly and how should I write my formula using the scaled R.

> dim(R)
[1] 1035 1035
> rank_R = rankMatrix(R)[1]
> rank_def = dim(R)[1] - rank_R
> rank_def
[1] 237
> egR = eigen(R)
> sum(egR$values<1e-12)
[1] 237
> A_null_egvector = egR$vectors[,-(1:rank_R)]
> dim(A_null_egvector)
[1] 1035  237
> Anew = t(A_null_egvector)

> R.scaled = inla.scale.model(R, constr = list(A = Anew, e=rep(0, nrow(Anew))))
x[.,.] <- val : x being coerced from Tsparse* to CsparseMatrix

> generalized_var = diag(INLA:::inla.ginv(R.scaled))
> exp(sum(log(generalized_var))/length(generalized_var))
[1] 1.000025

So I used the null space spanned by the null eigenvectors, does that make sense? I may try to read the related articles to figure out how those constraints come into play. 

A word about extra constrains in my model:
Clearly, the constraints I want to add in the f() will not make up the rank deficiency. However, that's enough for identification purpose.

Second part: since you mentioned I can just scale the precision matrix by the generalized variance. From my following tests, the conclusion is the three methods:
1. Calculate generalized inverse and multiple the precision
2. Provide full constraints if you know what are they, like in rw2 models, the sum-to-zero and the linear constraints will make up the rank deficiency 2 and used inla.scale.model to scale the matrix.
3. For complicated precision matrices, it's hard to think up the constraints. Instead, I provide the null space spanned by eigenvectors and then use inla.scale.model.

Conclusion: all those methods yield same results(<1e-6).

Question: What's the role of the constraints? The first method method looks more directly, but why inla.scale.model is often used with constraints.
library(INLA)
#method 1: calculate generalized variance

Q = INLA:::inla.rw(10, order = 2)
S = INLA:::inla.ginv(Q, rankdef = 2)
exp(mean(log(diag(S))))

s = exp(mean(log(diag(S))))
Q.scaled.1 = s * Q
S = INLA:::inla.ginv(Q.scaled.1, rankdef = 2)
exp(mean(log(diag(S))))#it's 1

#method 2: use build i function with constraints

Q = INLA:::inla.rw(10, order = 2)
constr = list(A = rbind(rep(1,10), 1:10), e = c(0,0))

Q.scaled.2 = inla.scale.model(Q, constr)

range(Q.scaled.1-Q.scaled.2)#[1] -9.304157e-06  1.395624e-05

#using eigen
Q = INLA:::inla.rw(10, order = 2)

null_vectors = eigen(Q)$vectors[,-(1:8)]#the last two columns coresponds to "zero" eigen values
#           [,1]        [,2]
# [1,] 0.00000000  0.58775381
# [2,] 0.05923489  0.49495058
# [3,] 0.11846978  0.40214735
# [4,] 0.17770466  0.30934411
# [5,] 0.23693955  0.21654088
# [6,] 0.29617444  0.12373764
# [7,] 0.35540933  0.03093441
# [8,] 0.41464421 -0.06186882
# [9,] 0.47387910 -0.15467206
# [10,] 0.53311399 -0.24747529
plot(1:10, null_vectors[,1])#it's actually the linear constraint, up to the scale constant
plot(1:10, null_vectors[,2])#Surprisingly, this one also matches 1:10
#So, where is the sum-to-zero constraint? rep(1,10)
Anew = t(null_vectors)
Q.scaled.3 = inla.scale.model(Q, constr = list(A = Anew, e=rep(0, nrow(Anew))))
generalized_var = diag(INLA:::inla.ginv(Q.scaled))
exp(sum(log(generalized_var))/length(generalized_var))#it's 1.000001
#this result is also the same
range(Q.scaled.1-Q.scaled.3)#[1] -9.309450e-06  1.396418e-05
Q.scaled.1[1,1] / Q[1]#1.818653
Q.scaled.2[1,1] / Q[1]#1.818651
Q.scaled.3[1,1] / Q[1]#1.818651


Again, thanks for you explanation. If possible, could you give me more insights what's going on? Or some references for me to figure them out.

Best,
Jiang

parts:
On Wed, 2017-12-20 at 00:05 -0800, Jiang Du wrote:
>
> Second part: since you mentioned I can just scale the precision
> matrix by the generalized variance. From my following tests, the
> conclusion is the three methods:
> 1. Calculate generalized inverse and multiple the precision
> 2. Provide full constraints if you know what are they, like in rw2
> models, the sum-to-zero and the linear constraints will make up the
> rank deficiency 2 and used inla.scale.model to scale the matrix.
> 3. For complicated precision matrices, it's hard to think up the
> constraints. Instead, I provide the null space spanned by
> eigenvectors and then use inla.scale.model.
>
> Conclusion: all those methods yield same results(<1e-6).
its all the same, so should give the same result, up to a small epsilon
> Question: What's the role of the constraints?

for the inla.scale.model the constraints are a basis for the null
space, and without that knowledge, we cannot do the scaling for huge
models efficiently.

> The first method method looks more directly, but why
> inla.scale.model is often used with constraints.

because its a O(n^(3/2)) cost instead of O(n^3). the direct one
(ginv()) is ok for smaller model but does not scale.

> Again, thanks for you explanation. If possible, could you give me
> more insights what's going on? Or some references for me to figure
> them out.

ch.3 in the GMRF book.

in most cases, this applies to intrinsic models as they are by nature, not scaled.
other proper models, are usually scaled, but not always, and then its easier to do so.

like the standard AR1

x_t = \phi x_{t-1} + \eps_t

with Prec(\eps_t) = \kappa

is NOT scaled as the marginal variance is 1/(1-\phi^2)/\kappa

in this case, we reparameterize it to be scaled, see inla.doc("ar1")


best

H

other proper models, are usually scaled, but not always, and then its easier to do so.

like the standard AR1

        x_t = \phi  x_{t-1} + \eps_t

with Prec(\eps_t) = \kappa

is NOT scaled as the marginal variance is 1/(1-\phi^2)/\kappa

in this case, we reparameterize it to be scaled, see inla.doc("ar1")
